About: how a uniform field changes the random path of one conduction electron, and the mean velocity of many

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the same electron path twice, top without a field (grey) and bottom in the field E pointing right (blue), on fixed axes x from −100 to 40 nm and y from −40 to 40 nm at equal scale, with a 10 nm scale bar and a dotted line through the start. Once question 1 is answered, an orange arrow shows the force −eE on the electron, opposite to E. Right: the mean velocity ⟨vx⟩ along E of 20 000 electrons against the time t since the field was switched on.
Controls
The field strength E (0, 2, 4 or 6 MV/m) and the mean free time τc (10 to 30 fs) restart the run on the same random sequence; New sequence draws a fresh sequence of kick directions and free times. Simulated time runs at 40 fs per second.
Measured
Every flight is exact constant-force motion from the latest kick, at 1.076 × 105 m/s, the classical mean thermal speed of an electron at 300 K. This is Drude's picture: in a real metal the conduction electrons move near the Fermi speed, about 106 m/s, and the mean free time is set by that. The drift velocity −eEτc/me does not depend on the kick speed. Δx is each electron's x from its start in nm, and the gap is their difference; ⟨vx⟩ is the plain mean over the 20 000 electrons in km/s. Their random velocities cancel exactly in mirror pairs, so ⟨vx⟩ is exactly 0 at t = 0 and stays 0 when E = 0. After that, the finite sample of collision times makes it wander from the smooth curve by a few per cent of the drift velocity, up to about 0.5 km/s at the largest E and τc.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two paths, with and without the field

Set E to 4 MV/m and τc to 20 fs; the run is ready at t = 0. Before pressing Play, predict how the path in the bottom panel, with the field, will differ from the path in the top panel. Then press Play, watch both paths to the end and compare the two readouts of Δx.

2 · When the gap grows

Keep E at 4 MV/m and τc at 20 fs; the run is ready at t = 0 again. You will press Play and watch the readout of the gap between the electron in the bottom panel and its twin in the top panel. Before pressing Play, predict when this gap grows most.

3 · New random sequences

Keep the settings of question 2. You will press New sequence and then Play several times, each time comparing where the two paths end. Before you do, predict what you will find.

4 · Many electrons at once

Set E to 2 MV/m and keep τc at 20 fs; the run is ready at t = 0. The field is switched on at t = 0 for the 20 000 electrons of the right-hand plot, whose velocities until then point equally in all directions. Before pressing Play, predict how ⟨vx⟩ will change. Then press Play and watch the plot and the readout of ⟨vx⟩.

5 · Double the field

Keep τc at 20 fs and note the steady value of ⟨vx⟩ at E = 2 MV/m, which stays in pale grey. Now set E to 4 MV/m. Before pressing Play, predict the new curve. Then press Play and compare the two curves.

6 · Halve the collision time

Keep E at 4 MV/m and set τc to 10 fs, so that the curve for 20 fs stays in pale grey. Before pressing Play, predict the new curve. Then press Play and compare the two curves.

7 · What to take away

Between collisions the field bends each flight very slightly. The force on an electron, −eE, points opposite to E, and its shifts only ever add in one direction, so a drift builds up beneath the random zigzag.

Averaged over many electrons, the field's gain balances the loss at collisions, and the mean velocity settles at the drift velocity vd = −eEτc/me within a time of order τc.

vd ∝ E is Ohm's law: the current density is J = −nevd = (ne2τc/me)E = σE. In an ordinary wire the drift is a small fraction of a millimetre per second; the fields here are about 108 times larger, to make it visible.

The Physics

The Path of a Conduction Electron · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim follows one electron in a metal through a random series of collisions, twice, with no field and with a field, and plots the mean velocity of 20 000 electrons beside it. You change the field and the time between collisions and compare.

What you'll learn

  • How a field changes the zigzag of a conduction electron.
  • When during its motion the change builds up.
  • How the mean velocity of many electrons depends on the field and on the collision time.
The set-up: an electron zigzags between collisions with the ions, and a field E points to the right.

What's on screen

  • Top panel, grey: the electron's path with no field. Dots mark the collisions.
  • Bottom panel, blue: the same electron on the same random sequence, with the field on.
  • Violet arrow: the field E, along +x, to the right.
  • Right plot: the mean velocity ⟨vx⟩ of 20 000 electrons against the time since the field was switched on.
  • Readouts: the time, the collisions, how far each path has moved in x, the gap between them and ⟨vx⟩.
See itLook at the set-up before the electron moves. Watch for: both paths at their start in the two panels, the violet arrow pointing right, and the right plot empty at ⟨vx⟩ = 0.

03

The force and the drift point opposite to the field

An electron has charge −e, so in the field E the force on it is −eE. It points opposite to E, and between collisions the electron accelerates at −eE/me (notes, Fig. 34). At E = 4 MV/m that is 7.0 × 1017 m/s², to the left in the sim, because E points right.

A flight lasts a time of order τc = 20 fs, so it is about 2.15 nm long. In that time the acceleration moves the electron only 0.14 nm sideways. Each path between collisions is a very slightly bent parabolic arc, and the notes call the drift in their figure greatly exaggerated.

One flight kicked across the field, E = 4 MV/m and τc = 20 fs. The bend is drawn ten times too large.

The collisions keep the zigzag. The field adds a small push, always to the left, to every flight.

See itPlay the two paths at E = 4 MV/m and τc = 20 fs (both are set for you). Watch for: the blue path ending to the left of its grey twin, with Gap, bottom − top turning negative.
04

The gap opens during the flights, most in the long ones

A collision gives the electron and its field-off twin the same new velocity, so no gap opens at a collision. In the flight that follows, the field alone shifts the electron to the left of its twin by

eEt2 / 2me
Here t is the time since the last collision.

The shift grows as t². A flight twice as long opens a gap four times as big. At E = 4 MV/m a flight of t = τc = 20 fs shifts the electron by 0.14 nm, and a flight of 3τc shifts it by 1.27 nm, nine times as much.

Shift from the field-off twin against flight time, E = 4 MV/m. Dots: t = τc, 2τc and 3τc.

Flight times are random, with mean τc, so a few long flights open much of the gap and the short ones add little.

See itPlay the paths again at E = 4 MV/m and τc = 20 fs and follow the gap. Watch for: Gap, bottom − top falling steadily through a long flight, and hardly at all through a short one.
05

Every sequence ends behind its twin

Every flight shifts the electron left of its twin and none shifts it right, so the shifts only add. The gap is the sum of the 40 flight shifts. The mean of t2 is 2τc2, because every electron has the same chance dt/τc of colliding in each short interval dt (notes). Each flight therefore shifts the electron by 0.28 nm on average, and over 40 flights the expected gap is 11.3 nm to the left.

The random wander shared by both twins is larger. For 40 flights at τc = 20 fs its spread along x is about 14 nm. So in some sequences, roughly one in five, both paths end to the right of the start. The blue path still ends to the left of the grey one.

Key idea. The field decides which twin ends behind. The random sequence decides where each ends, and by how much.
See itDraw a new sequence at E = 4 MV/m and τc = 20 fs, and play it. Watch for: the blue path ending to the left of the grey path, wherever each one ends.
06

The mean velocity levels off at the drift velocity

The right plot follows 20 000 electrons. Before the field is switched on their velocities point equally in all directions, so ⟨vx⟩ = 0. In a short time dt the field adds momentum −eE dt to every electron, and a fraction dt/τc of them collide and lose the mean momentum mevd they carry. So the mean velocity vd obeys

me dvd/dt = −eE − mevd/τc
Equation (4.15). The same form as a body falling with linear drag.

It settles when the two terms balance, at the drift velocity

vd = −eEτc / me
Equation (4.16).

The approach is vd(1 − e−t/τc), reaching 63% of vd at t = τc and 95% at 3τc. At E = 2 MV/m and τc = 20 fs, vd = −7.0 km/s.

⟨vx⟩ against t at E = 2 MV/m, τc = 20 fs. The dashed line is vd.
See itPlay the 20 000 electrons at E = 2 MV/m and τc = 20 fs. Watch for: ⟨vx⟩ falling from 0 and levelling off near −7.0 km/s within about 60 fs.
07

The drift is proportional to E and τc, which is Ohm’s law

The level −eEτc/me is proportional to E, and the time to reach it is of order τc, which the field does not change. At τc = 20 fs, E = 2, 4 and 6 MV/m give −7.0, −14.1 and −21.1 km/s. The level is also proportional to τc: at E = 4 MV/m, τc = 10 fs gives −7.0 km/s, reached in half the time.

⟨vx⟩ against t for three settings. Dashed lines: vd.

In a metal the current density is J = −nee vd. With (4.16), J = σcE, where

σc = nee2τc / me
Equation (4.17). The sim does not set ne.

J proportional to E is Ohm’s law, and it holds because τc does not depend on E.

E τc

These sliders move the sim too. The number comes from the sim's own function.

See itPlay E = 2 MV/m, then double the field to 4 MV/m while keeping τc = 20 fs. Watch for: the pale curve for 2 MV/m staying put, and the new curve levelling off at twice the value in about the same time.
See itPlay E = 4 MV/m, then halve the collision time to 10 fs. Watch for: the pale curve for 20 fs staying put, and the new curve levelling off at half the value in half the time.
08

Where it matters

  • The drift is slow. In a wire of cross-section A carrying a current I, the drift speed is I/(neeA), very much smaller than the mean electron speed because ne is so large (notes, Problem 5). The sim uses fields about 108 times those in ordinary wires so that the drift can be drawn.
  • The kick speed does not matter. The sim starts each flight at the classical thermal speed, 1.076 × 105 m/s. In a real metal the electrons move near the Fermi speed, about 106 m/s, and vd = −eEτc/me is the same.
  • The model has limits. With the mean speed √(8kB𝒯/πme) and a mean free path fixed by the ion spacing, it gives a resistivity that goes as 𝒯1/2. In a pure metal near room temperature it is close to proportional to 𝒯. The quantum theory of electrons in metals is not treated in the notes.
09

Summary

In one line. A field acts on a conduction electron between its collisions, and the sim follows what that does to one electron's path and to the mean velocity of many.
  • The force −eE points opposite to E. It bends each flight slightly, by eEt²/2me, and the shifts all add in one direction.
  • The mean velocity levels off at vd = −eEτc/me within a time of order τc.
  • vd is proportional to E, so J = σcE: Ohm’s law.

Common mix-ups

  • "The field carries the electron along E." The charge is −e, so the force and the drift point opposite to E.
  • "The gap opens at the collisions." A collision gives both twins the same velocity. The gap opens during the flights.
  • "A stronger field reaches its drift sooner." The time is set by τc. Doubling E doubles the level in about the same time.

Things to try on your own

  • Set E = 0 and play. Compare the two paths and ⟨vx⟩.
  • At τc = 30 fs, find vd for E = 2 MV/m and check it against the plot.
  • Press New sequence five times and note where each path ends compared with its twin.
